clue.text: One for placing behind the silver?

definitions.text: One for placing behind the silver?

blocks.clueFragment: One for placing behind the silver?
blocks.note: surface reading: something set at the back of the silverware, as on a sideboard
setter's reading: the medal for the place that comes after second

explanation.surface: Someone arranging the family silver asks what goes at the back of the display.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Placing' sounds like putting an object somewhere; in a race it is a finishing position, and third place earns the medal after silver.
explanation.definitionFit: In sport, the third-placed finisher receives a medal of this copper-tin alloy, ranked just below the silver one.

clue.text: In August, a stag with lots of points and a beard

definitions.text: a stag with lots of points

blocks.note: first meaning: majestic, befitting an emperor

blocks.clueFragment: a stag with lots of points
blocks.note: second meaning: a red deer stag whose antlers carry fourteen points
third meaning: a small pointed tuft of beard under the lower lip, after Napoleon III

explanation.surface: A hunter recalls stalking a grand antlered stag one August, and growing a beard on the trip.
explanation.walkthrough: Three separate meanings of one word; the capital on 'August' hides the adjective meaning grand, not the month.
explanation.definitionFit: The word means majestic or emperor-like, names a fourteen-point stag in deer-stalking jargon, and names a goatee-style chin tuft.

clue.text: Trump extremely liable to be disturbing

definitions.note: the answer is the verb 'disturb'; with 'to be' read as a link the swap is loose

indicators.note: extremely points to the extremities of the next word, its first and last letters

blocks.note: to ruff is to play a trump card in a suit you cannot follow
the two end letters of the word

explanation.surface: A political jibe: the former president is very likely to be unsettling.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Trump' looks like the politician, but it is the card-game verb; a ruff is the play of a trump.
explanation.definitionFit: To ruffle someone is to upset or unsettle their composure, the same idea as disturbing them.

clue.text: Hide in a corner of Greek island

blocks.note: the south-east corner, as on a map
the largest Greek island

explanation.surface: Someone goes into hiding in a remote corner of a Greek island.
explanation.walkthrough: 'In' looks like it places one thing inside another, but here it only joins definition to wordplay.
explanation.definitionFit: To secrete something is to conceal it in a hiding place, a less common sense beside the glandular one.

clue.text: Old lady on airline to India — where exactly?

definitions.note: a cryptic pointer: the answer is a precise place within India

blocks.note: 'old lady' is slang for mother
British Airways
I is India in the NATO phonetic alphabet

explanation.surface: A mother is flying to India, and someone asks which city exactly.
explanation.walkthrough: 'India' does double duty in the surface: it supplies the last letter and tells you the city is somewhere in that country.
explanation.definitionFit: The question asks for a precise location in India, and this western coastal city, formerly Bombay, is one.

clue.text: In short test, four or six quiz questions perhaps

indicators.note: short means the word is cut, losing its final letter
In tells us the number goes inside the shortened word

blocks.note: a trial is a test
Roman four; Roman six, VI, works equally well at a different spot

explanation.surface: A cricketer's short Test innings is summed up in fours and sixes, the sort of thing pub quizzes ask.
explanation.walkthrough: The clue lets you choose: IV inside TR_IA or VI inside TRI_A both give the same letters, hence 'four or six'.
explanation.definitionFit: Trivia are odd little facts of the kind pub quiz rounds are built on, so quiz questions are an example.

clue.text: Popular schoolgirl royally entertained at the Albert Hall?

definitions.text: royally entertained at the Albert Hall?

blocks.note: first meaning: the girl elected queen of a high-school dance

blocks.clueFragment: royally entertained at the Albert Hall?
blocks.note: second meaning, playful: a monarch enjoying a Prom concert, as the BBC Proms are held at the Royal Albert Hall

explanation.surface: A popular girl from school has a VIP night at a concert in the Albert Hall.
explanation.walkthrough: The BBC Proms are a summer series of classical concerts in London's Royal Albert Hall; a queen at one is literally a Prom queen.
explanation.definitionFit: In American schools the most popular senior girl is often crowned at the end-of-year dance, called the prom.

clue.text: Keep one article away from us

indicators.note: taking things away from a word means removing those letters from it

blocks.note: Roman numeral one
the indefinite article
the setter writes for this newspaper, so 'us' is the paper

explanation.surface: A warning to keep some unnamed item out of our reach.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Us' is the self-reference trick of this paper's puzzles: it names the newspaper. Remove I and AN from its end.
explanation.definitionFit: To keep something safe is to protect or watch over it, a straightforward verb synonym.

clue.text: Sack employees in insufficient numbers, getting attacked?

definitions.note: the answer is a phrase meaning 'being attacked'

blocks.note: under- as a prefix means too few or too little
to fire staff is to sack them

explanation.surface: A boss who lays off too few staff is criticised for it.
explanation.walkthrough: Read whimsically, to under-fire would be to sack too few people; the pieces are put in reverse of clue order.
explanation.definitionFit: A phrase from battle, being shot at, used figuratively for anyone facing heavy criticism.

clue.text: A bishop finished, almost — in heaven?

indicators.note: almost means not quite all of the word, so its last letter is dropped

blocks.note: taken as written
B is the chess notation for bishop
over means finished

explanation.surface: A bishop has nearly died and is wondering whether he is in heaven.
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark flags that 'in heaven' is a loose, example-style definition: heaven is traditionally up there.
explanation.definitionFit: Heaven is conventionally pictured overhead, so whatever is there lies over us, in the sky.

clue.text: Drink too much to exercise

blocks.note: taken as written
physical education, the school subject

explanation.surface: Advice that drinking heavily is a way to keep fit.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Too much' seems to be about drinking and exercise together, but the definition stops at 'much'.
explanation.definitionFit: To tope is an old-fashioned verb for drinking alcohol heavily and habitually; a toper is a drunkard.

clue.text: Mechanism to eliminate sex crime?

definitions.note: the answer read as a made-up verb DE-VICE

blocks.note: first meaning: a gadget or contrivance
second, whimsical meaning: to remove vice, the term for immoral crime policed by a vice squad

explanation.surface: Someone asks about a gadget for stamping out sexual offences.
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark signals the invented verb: like de-ice, de-vice would mean to clear away vice.
explanation.definitionFit: A device is a contrivance made for a particular purpose, a straightforward synonym for a mechanism.

clue.text: Crop tail, suffering in such heat

definitions.note: the answer is an adjective describing the heat; 'in' is a link

indicators.note: something suffering is in a bad way, damaged and out of its proper order

blocks.note: the eight letters of these two words

explanation.surface: An animal's docked tail is suffering in the heat.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Crop tail' reads as a command to dock an animal; the words are just letters to rearrange.
explanation.definitionFit: The fierce, humid heat of the regions near the equator is described with this adjective.

clue.text: Converse about the French holiday home

indicators.note: about means going around, so the first word wraps the second

blocks.note: to converse is to chat
the French masculine word for 'the'

explanation.surface: A chat about French holiday homes.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Converse' is the verb (to talk), not the shoe brand or the noun meaning opposite.
explanation.definitionFit: A chalet is a wooden Alpine-style house, often rented by holidaymakers, especially skiers.

clue.text: See 14
Local speech day: smart chap opens it

indicators.note: opening something means getting inside it, so the chap goes into the word that follows

blocks.note: standard abbreviation for day
taken as written
a smart alec is a know-all

explanation.surface: A clever man opens proceedings on a day devoted to regional speech.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Smart chap' is the phrase 'smart alec' with the name cut off.
explanation.definitionFit: A dialect is the variety of a language spoken in a particular region, with its own words and grammar.

clue.text: Woman entitled to conceal a grand loss

indicators.note: to conceal is to hide something inside, so the title holds the next letters

blocks.note: a Dame is a woman with that honorary title
a, plus G for grand, slang for a thousand pounds

explanation.surface: A titled lady hides that she has lost a thousand pounds.
explanation.walkthrough: A dame is the female equivalent of a knight in the British honours system; 'grand' is slang for a thousand.
explanation.definitionFit: Damage is harm or loss suffered, as in insurance claims for loss and damage.

clue.text: See 16
Inclination to talk hypocritically

blocks.note: first meaning: a slope or tilt
second meaning: to speak pious words you do not mean

explanation.surface: Someone has a tendency to speak insincerely.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Inclination' looks like a tendency or wish, but it means a physical slant.
explanation.definitionFit: The noun names a slope or bevel, and the verb means to utter sanctimonious, insincere moralising.

clue.text: Top tune, two consecutive notes short

blocks.note: D and E sit next to each other in the musical scale
scant means barely enough

explanation.surface: A hit melody that falls two notes short.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Top tune' suggests a chart hit, but it is the descant, the highest melodic line above a hymn.
explanation.definitionFit: A descant is a decorative melody sung or played above the main tune, so it sits at the top.

clue.text: One bearing stripes from such punishment?

blocks.note: first meaning: an army rank shown by two chevrons on the sleeve
second meaning: the adjective in the phrase for punishment by beating

explanation.surface: A victim covered in weals after being flogged.
explanation.walkthrough: The stripes look like lash marks from a beating; they are also the chevrons of an army rank.
explanation.definitionFit: The noun is a non-commissioned officer wearing two stripes; the adjective means of the body, as in physical punishment.

clue.text: Area of Europe crumbling into sea

indicators.note: something crumbling falls to pieces, and the letters reform in a new order

blocks.note: the letters of both words

explanation.surface: Part of the continent's coastline is eroding into the sea.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Area' covers a country loosely; the fodder is the two words after the signal.
explanation.definitionFit: Estonia is a Baltic country in north-east Europe, so it is a region of that continent.

clue.text: Appointments — mine gets rearranged

indicators.note: rearranged says these letters are to be set in a different order

blocks.note: the letters of both words

explanation.surface: Someone complains that their diary of engagements keeps being moved around.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface is almost literal: rescheduled appointments are rearranged meetings.
explanation.definitionFit: Meetings are arranged engagements to see people, which is what appointments are.

clue.text: Stretch old canvas

blocks.note: ex- means former
a tent is made of canvas, and campers say 'under canvas'

explanation.surface: An instruction to pull an old painting's canvas taut over its frame.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Stretch' reads as a verb for canvas on a frame; it is the noun, an expanse.
explanation.definitionFit: An extent is a stretch or expanse of space, as in the full extent of the estate.

clue.text: Also related being deceived

blocks.note: too means also
kin means family, related by blood

explanation.surface: A relative, as well, turned out to have been fooled.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition is the past tense; read the clue as 'deceived', with 'being' a joining word.
explanation.definitionFit: To take someone in is to fool them, so the past-tense phrasal verb means deceived.

clue.text: Group of artists urgently enthusiastic?

blocks.note: RA, the Royal Academy, or a Royal Academician
a ring is a group, as of conspirators

explanation.surface: A collective of painters is impatient to get going.
explanation.walkthrough: The Royal Academy of Arts in London gives the standard abbreviation RA for artists.
explanation.definitionFit: Raring, as in 'raring to go', describes someone eager and impatient to start, an idiom of keenness.

clue.text: To be given a lift not initially approved of

indicators.note: not initially means without the opening letter of the word

blocks.note: praised means spoken of with approval

explanation.surface: A hitchhiker is refused a ride by those who disapprove.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Lift' tempts as a car ride, but here it means being raised up.
explanation.definitionFit: Something lifted has been raised, the plain past participle synonym.

clue.text: Sexless: imagine uterus partially removed

indicators.note: only part of the following words is taken out of them, a run of letters lifted from inside

blocks.note: a run of letters across the two words

explanation.surface: A gruesome surgical scenario: picture a womb partly cut out.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Partially removed' reads as surgery; it tells you a part of the next words is lifted out.
explanation.definitionFit: Neuter means neither male nor female, without sexual organs, as with a neutered animal.

clue.text: Glasses of wine knocked back in bad temper

indicators.note: knocked back plays on downing a drink, and sending it back means reading it backwards

blocks.note: port is a fortified wine

explanation.surface: Someone downs glasses of wine in a foul mood.
explanation.walkthrough: A strop is British slang for a sulk or fit of bad temper.
explanation.definitionFit: Being in a strop means sulking or being in a fit of pique, an informal British idiom.

clue.text: Speech to which no one replies

definitions.text: Speech to which no one replies

blocks.clueFragment: Speech to which no one replies
blocks.note: surface reading: an address so dull or unanswerable that it gets no response
setter's reading: nobody can reply because the speaker is alone on stage, talking to himself

explanation.walkthrough: It sounds like a speech met with silence; in drama it is a speech nobody else hears, like Hamlet's 'To be or not to be'.
explanation.definitionFit: A speech a character delivers alone on stage, voicing private thoughts, which by convention no other character answers.

clue.text: Householder making very slow progress

blocks.note: surface reading: a homeowner taking forever over something, perhaps a renovation
setter's reading: a creature that literally carries its house on its back

explanation.walkthrough: 'Householder' suggests a property owner; read literally, it is someone who holds a house, the shelled creature that crawls.
explanation.definitionFit: This garden mollusc carries its shell as a home and moves proverbially slowly.

clue.text: Getting into Emirates improperly, very short cut

indicators.note: done improperly means done wrongly, so the letters come out in the wrong order
getting into means entering, so one letter goes inside the rearranged ones

blocks.note: standard abbreviation for very
the letters of the word

explanation.surface: Someone sneaks onto an Emirates flight improperly, taking a very short cut.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Emirates' suggests the airline, but it is just the eight letters to rearrange around V.
explanation.definitionFit: A short cut saves time, so it is a time-saving device or method.
